artworks.title: Farnese Bull
artworks.artist: Apollonius of Tralles and Tauriscus of Tralles
artworks.description: The colossal marble group in Naples — Amphion and Zethus binding Dirce to the bull that will drag her to death — is antiquity's most famous image of the Theban queen's punishment. Found in the Baths of Caracalla and restored in the Renaissance, it made Dirce's cruelty and doom a landmark of Roman sculpture.

artworks.title: Dirce
artworks.description: Bartolini's Louvre marble reduces the Farnese drama to a single bound nude — Dirce alone, ropes and bull implied, Neoclassical pathos instead of Hellenistic crowd. The reduced version for the Duke of Devonshire kept the Theban torment in nineteenth-century salons.

artworks.title: Christian Dirce
artworks.description: Siemiradzki's National Museum in Warsaw canvas restages Nero's arena as a 'Dircean' spectacle: a Christian woman tied to a bull before a glittering Roman crowd. The painting turns the mythic punishment into a modern indictment — Dirce's death as template for imperial cruelty.

popCulture.title: Dirce
popCulture.description: Wife of Lycus, tormentor of Antiope — her bull-bound death became Thebes' spring and sculpture's most famous Theban crime.
